###### Abstract

This paper deals with the problem of designing a sampled-data state feedback control law for continuous-time linear control systems subject to uniform input quantization. The sampled-data state feedback is designed in order to ensure uniform global asymptotic stability (UGAS) of an attractor surrounding the origin. The closed-loop system is rewritten as a hybrid dynamical system. To do this, an auxiliary clock variable triggering the occurrence of sampling events is introduced. A numerically tractable algorithm with feasibility guarantees, based on concave-convex decomposition, is then proposed allowing to minimize the size of the attractor. Theoretical results are illustrated in a numerical example.

Quantized control, sampled-data systems, LMIs, stability, hybrid systems.

1. INTRODUCTION

C. Shelby[1] AEFC

The design of a new generation of control systems combining physical interactions with computational and communication abilities presents strong advantages in terms of scalability, maintenance, and computational resources, for example for transportation systems, autonomous robotics, and energy delivery systems (Murray et al. (2002)). This paper focuses on one of these digital elements, namely, quantization, which is typically used to reduce data traffic load in communication channels to comply with limited bandwidth constraints. As a side effect, quantization induces a nonlinear behavior into the closed loop. See, for example, Delchamps et al. (1990), Ceragioli et al. (2011), Liberzon et al. (2003b), Tarbouriech and Gouaisbaut (2012). Most of the works dealing with quantized control systems focus either on continuous-time systems (Brockett and Liberzon (2000), Liberzon (, (1998), Fridman and Dambrine (2009), Ferrante et al. (2015), Ferrante et al. (2020)), or on discrete-time systems, (Picasso and Colaneri (2008), Fu and Xie (2009), Campos et al. (2018), Ichihara et al. (2018)). However, in many applications the actual setting consists of a physical plant that is controlled via a digital controller. Because the dynamics of the physical plants are naturally described by continuous-time systems, the resulting closed-loop system turns out to be a sampled-data system. Sampled-data systems have been extensively studied in the last twenty years; see Hetel et al. (2017) for a recent survey on sampled-data systems. One might argue that the impact of quantization in sampled-data systems may be studied by relying on a discretized model of the plant. However, by pursuing this approach the analysis of the intersample behavior is completely lost.

Despite the fact that quantization and sampling naturally coexist, surprisingly not much attention has been devoted to the control design of quantized sampled-data systems. The interplay of sampling and quantization has been analyzed in Nesic and Liberzon (2009). Therein, a unified framework for controller design in the presence of quantization and time scheduling based on an emulation approach is investigated. Stabilization of sampled-data systems with stochastic sampling times in the presence of logarithmic input quantization has been addressed in Shen et al. (2017) by relying on a discretized model of the closed-loop system. Recently, robust sampled-data stabilization in the presence of input/state quantization and uncertainties for a rather general class nonlinear systems has been studied in Di Ferrandino et al. (2021), where the authors provide sufficient conditions for semiglobal practical asymptotic stability in the presence of fast sampling and accurate quantization.

In this paper, we consider a setup in which a linear plant is controlled via a periodic uniformly quantized sampled-data state feedback controller. In contrast with Shen et al. (2017) and with the objective of fully characterizing the intersample behavior of the closed-loop system, we model the closed loop as a hybrid dynamical system in the framework of Goebel et al. (2012). Within this setting, we provide sufficient conditions for uniform global asymptotic stability of a compact set containing the origin of the plant substate. These conditions are later used to devise a design algorithm for the controller to mitigate the impact of input quantization on the closed-loop state. It is noteworthy to mention that, as opposed to Di Ferlandino et al. (2021), we assume that the quantization error bound and the

### 2.3 Basic properties of \(\mathcal{H}_{cl}\) and Krasovskii regularization

In this subsection, we illustrate some structural properties of hybrid model \(\mathcal{H}_{cl}\).

**Property 1.** For hybrid system \(\mathcal{H}_{cl}\), the following properties holds:

(i) For any \(\xi \in \mathcal{C} \cup \mathcal{D}\), there exists a nontrivial solution \(\phi\) to \(\mathcal{H}_{cl}\) with \(\phi(0,0) = \xi\); (ii) Any maximal solution to \(\mathcal{H}_{cl}\) is complete; (iii) Any complete solution \(\phi\) is \(t\)-complete, i.e., \(\text{sup}_{t}\text{dom}\phi = \infty\).

**Proof.** The proof hinges upon direct application of (Goebel et al., 2012, Proposition 2.10, page 33). In particular, the viability condition (VC) in (Goebel et al., 2012, Proposition 2.10, page 33) trivially holds on \(\mathcal{C} \backslash \mathcal{D} = \mathbb{R}^{n_p} \times \mathbb{R}^{n_u} \times [0, T]\) due to the flow dynamics being affine and the dynamics of \(\tau\) allowing flows when \(\tau \in [0, T)\). This yields item (i). To show item (ii), still from (Goebel et al., 2012, Proposition 2.10, page 33), since no finite escape times are possible and \(g(\mathcal{D}) \subset \mathcal{C}\), item (ii) follows directly. To conclude the proof, observe that \(g(\mathcal{D}) \subset (\mathcal{C} \backslash \mathcal{D})\). Moreover, the timer dynamics (4) ensure that the length of any flow interval is lower bounded by \(T\). Thus, item (iii) follows.

The above result shows that hybrid system \(\mathcal{H}_{cl}\) is well behaved in terms of existence and completeness of (maximal) solutions. However, the discontinuity of the map \(\psi_{\Delta}\) prevents \(\mathcal{H}_{cl}\) from fulfilling the so-called hybrid basic conditions; see (Goebel et al., 2012, Assumption 6.5, page 120). Hybrid systems not fulfilling the hybrid basic conditions may be overly sensitive to small vanishing noise. Moreover, the fulfillment of the hybrid basic conditions is a key ingredient for the application of several important results. To overcome this problem, in this paper we consider the so-called Krasovskii regularization of \(\mathcal{H}_{cl}\); see (Goebel et al., 2012, Definition 4.13, page 81). This regularization basically corresponds to the “smallest” hybrid dynamical systems containing \(\mathcal{H}_{cl}\) fulfilling the hybrid basic conditions. In the specific case of hybrid system \(\mathcal{H}_{cl}\), such a regularization writes as:

\[\mathcal{H}_{cl} \doteq \{x = f(x), \quad x \in \mathcal{C}\] (6)

\[\{x^{+} \in G(x), \quad x \in \mathcal{D}\] (7)

where for all \(x \in \mathcal{D}\)

\[G(x) := \bigcap_{\delta > 0} g((x + \delta\mathbb{B}) \cap \mathcal{D}).\] (8)

Because \(g\) is locally bounded on \(\mathcal{D}\), similarly as in (Bacciotti, 2004, Lemma 1), it is easy to see that for all \(x \in \mathcal{D}\):

\[G(x) = \{v \in \mathbb{R}^{n_p + n_u + 1} : \exists\{x_k\} \subset \mathcal{D}\] \[s.t. x_k \to x, g(x_k) \to v\} .\] (9)

Using the above equivalent rewriting of \(G\), simple continuity arguments yield:

\[G(x) = \begin{bmatrix} (G_{cl} + J_{cl} K) \xi + J_{cl} \Phi(\xi) \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \forall x \in \mathcal{D}\] (10)

where for all \(\xi \in \mathbb{R}^{n_p + n_u}\):

\[\Phi(\xi) := \bigcap_{\delta \succ 0} \underbrace{\psi_{\Delta} (K(\xi+\delta\mathbb{B}))}_{\delta > 0}.\] (11)

It is worth to observe that since \(g(\mathcal{D}) \subset G(\mathcal{D})\), solutions to hybrid system (5) are solutions to (6). Therefore, stability properties established for (6), among others, carry over directly to (5). Moreover, completeness of maximal solutions to (6) is still ensured.

To simplify the analysis of the closed-loop system, we over-approximate the set-valued map \(\Phi\) via the following inclusion:

\[\Phi(\xi) \subset \Psi_{\Delta}(K\xi), \quad \forall \xi \in \mathbb{R}^{n_p + n_u}.\] (12)

where \(\Psi_{\Delta}\) is the Krasovskii regularization of the mapping \(\psi_{\Delta}\), namely:

\[\Psi_{\Delta}(u) := \bigcap_{\delta > 0} \underbrace{\psi_{\Delta} (u + \delta\mathbb{B})}_{\delta > 0}, \quad \forall u \in \mathbb{R}^{n_u}.\] (13)

In particular, (12) can be proven directly by relying on the continuity of the function \(\xi \mapsto K\xi\). It is worth to observe that, since \(g(\mathcal{D}) \subset G(\mathcal{D})\), solutions to hybrid system (5) are solutions to (6). Therefore, stability properties established for (6), among others, carry over directly to (5). Moreover, due to \(G(\mathcal{D}) \subset (\mathcal{C} \backslash \mathcal{D})\), completeness and non-Zenoness of maximal solutions to (6) follows from similar arguments as in the proof of Property 1.

At this stage, it is important to observe that, due to the presence of input quantization, generally asymptotic stabilization of the origin of the \(\xi\)-substate cannot be achieved. Indeed, roughly speaking, due to \(\psi_{\Delta}\) being zero around zero, the closed-loop system behaves in open loop near the origin. Therefore, it is natural to turn the attention towards asymptotic stability of a “possibly minimal” compact set \(\mathcal{A} \subset \mathbb{R}^{n_p + n_u+1}\) containing the origin of the \(\xi\)-substate. This leads to the following statement for the stabilization problem we solve in this paper.

**Problem 1.** (Stabilization). Design a gain \(K\) such that there exists a compact set \(\mathcal{A} \subset \mathbb{R}^{n_p + n_u + 1}\) such that the following hold:

(a) \((\{0_{n_p}\} \times \{0_{n_u}\} \times [0, T]) \subset \mathcal{A};\)

(b) \(\mathcal{A}\) is uniformly globally asymptotically stable UGAS for hybrid system (6).

4. CONTROLLER DESIGN

In this section, we show how the results developed in Section 3 can be exploited to devise a design algorithm for the solution to Problem 1 based on semidefinite programming. In particular, the implicit objective of Problem 1 is to design a controller gain \(K\) minimizing the size of the attractor \(\mathcal{A}\) defined in (14). In this regard, it is worth to observe that for the attractor \(\mathcal{A}\) in (14) the following chain of inclusions holds:

\[\mathcal{A} \subset \underbrace{\left(\bigcup_{\tau \in [0,T]} \mathcal{E} \left( \exp(A_{cl} \tau) \right)^\top P \exp(A_{cl} \tau) \right)}_{\mathcal{O}} \times [0,T]\] (21) \[(\overset{\circ}{\square} \mathcal{E}(\omega \lambda_{\min} (P) I) \times [0,T])\]

with

\[\omega := \min_{\tau \in [0,T]} \lambda_{\min} \left( \exp(A_{cl} \tau) \right)^\top \exp(A_{cl} \tau).\]

This shows that, \(\overline{\omega}\) being fixed, the attractor \(\mathcal{A}\) can be shrunk by maximizing \(\lambda_{\min} (P)\). In particular, this naturally leads to formulate Problem 1 as the following optimization problem:

\[\begin{array}{ll}
\underset{P, K, S_{1}, S_{2}, \theta, c}{\text{maximize}} & c \\
\text{subject to} & P - cl \geq 0, (12) - (13) \\
& \theta \geq 0, P \in \mathbb{S}_{++}^{n + n_{c}}, S_{1}, S_{2} \in \mathbb{D}_{++}^{n_{u}} \\
& K \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{u} \times (n_{p} + n_{u})}.
\end{array}
(22)\]

It is important to observe that due to (20) being bilinear in the decision variables, (22) is numerically intractable. To overcome this problem, in this paper we rely on the approach proposed in Dinh et al. (2011) to suboptimally solve (22) via a sequence of semidefinite programming (SDP) problems, i.e., optimization problems with linear objective over linear matrix inequality constraints. To deploy this approach, as a first step we rewrite (20) in the following equivalent linear-bilinear decomposed form:

\[\mathcal{L}(P, S_{1}, S_{2}) + \mathrm{He}(\mathcal{X}^\top (\theta, K) \mathcal{V}(P, S_{2})) \prec 0,\]

with

\[\mathcal{L}(P, S_{1}, S_{2}) := \begin{bmatrix} -P & 0 & G_{cl}^\top (\mathcal{V}(P))\\ \star & -S_{1} - 2S_{2} & J_{cl}^\top (\mathcal{V}(P))\\ \star & \star & -I(\mathcal{V}(P))\end{bmatrix},\]

\[\mathcal{X}^\top (\theta, K) := \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\beta}{2}I & K^\top\\ 0 & 0\\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \mathcal{Y}(P, S_{2}) := \begin{bmatrix} P & 0 & 0\\ 0 & -S_{2} & J_{cl}^\top (\mathcal{V}(P))\end{bmatrix}.\]

The latter, dropping the dependency on the decision variables, can be equivalently rewritten in the following psd convex-concave decomposed form; see (Dinh et al., 2011, Definition 2.1):

\[\mathcal{L} + \mathcal{X}^\top \mathcal{X} + \mathcal{Y}^\top \mathcal{Y} - (\mathcal{X} - \mathcal{Y})^\top (\mathcal{X} - \mathcal{Y}) \prec 0\]

which, by Schur complement's lemma, is equivalent to:

\[\begin{bmatrix} \mathcal{L} - \mathcal{X}^\top \mathcal{X} - \mathcal{Y}^\top \mathcal{Y} + \mathrm{He}(\mathcal{X}^\top \mathcal{Y}) & \mathcal{X}^\top & \mathcal{Y}^\top\\ \star & -I & 0\\ \star & \star & -I \end{bmatrix} \prec 0.
(23)\]

Based on the equivalent rewriting of (20) in (23), the following "linear inner approximation" of optimization problem (22) around the point \(\eta^{(0)} = (\varrho^{(0)}, P^{(0)}, K^{(0)}, S_2^{(0)}) \in \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{S}_{++}^{n_p + n_u} \times [\mathbb{R}^{n_{u} \times (n_p + n_u)} (x) \times \mathcal{D}_{++}^{n_u}]\) is considered:

\[\begin{array}{ll}
O^{(0)}: & \begin{array}{ll} \underset{P, K, S_1, S_2, \theta, c}{\text{maximize}} & c \\ \text{s.t.} & \mathcal{M}(P, S_1, S_2, K, \theta \eta^{(0)}) \prec 0, \\
& \Delta^\top S_{1} \Delta - \theta \leq 0\\ & P - cI \succeq 0, \theta \in (0, 1)\end{array}\\
& \Rightarrow \mathcal{L} \in \mathbb{S}_{++}^{n_p + n_u}, S_{1}, S_{2} \in \mathbb{D}_{++}^{n_u}.
\end{array}\]

where:

\[\begin{array}{ll}
\mathcal{R}(P, S_{1}, S_{2}, K, \theta \eta^{(0)}) & W(\theta, P, S_{2}, K)\\ &= \frac{(\mathcal{M}(P, S_{1}, S_{2}, K, \theta \eta^{(0)}) - I)}{-I},
\end{array}\]

where:

\[\left[\frac{\mathcal{R}(P, S_{1}, S_{2}, K, \theta \eta^{(0)}) - \mathcal{L}(P, S_{1}, S_{2}, P) + \mathcal{Q}(\eta^{(0)}) + (\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{Q}(\eta^{(0)})))(\theta - \theta^{(0)}, P - P^{(0)}, K - K^{(0)}, S_{2} - S_2^\top)}{W(\theta, P, S_{2}, K)^\top \mathcal{M}(P, S_{1}, S_{2}, K)} \right],
\]

in which

\[\begin{array}{ll}
(\theta, P, K, S_{2}) \mapsto \mathcal{Q}(\theta, P, S_{2}, K) & := -\mathcal{X}^\top \mathcal{X} - \mathcal{Y}^\top \mathcal{Y} + \mathrm{He}(\mathcal{X}^\top \mathcal{Y}).\end{array}\]

At this stage, provided that an initial feasible solution \(\eta^{(0)}\) to optimization problem (22) is available, \(O^{(0)}\) is solved. This, due to the property of psd-convex functions; see (Dinh et al., 2011, Lemma 2.1, item (b)), generates another feasible solution to optimization problem (22). Then, the process is repeated, thereby giving rise to a sequence of SDP problems. The applicability of this approach requires the knowledge of an initial feasible solution to optimization problem (22), which is basically used to generate the sequence of SDP problems \(\{O^{(k)}\}\). To this end, we make use of the following result.

**6. CONCLUSION**

The problem of designing a sampled-data state feedback control law for continuous-time linear control systems subject to uniform input quantization was addressed. The main goal was to design a sampled-data state feedback to ensure uniform global asymptotic stability (UGAS) of a compact set containing the origin of the plant substate. The closed loop was augmented with an auxiliary clock

Variable triggering the occurrence of sampling events and modeled as a hybrid dynamical system. Sufficient conditions for stability in the form of bilinear matrix inequalities were proposed. An iterative algorithm based on the use of the convex-concave decomposition approach was proposed to design an optimal controller with the objective of minimizing the size of the closed-loop attractor. Under some mild conditions on the open-loop system, the proposed design algorithm was shown to be deadlock free. The interest of the proposed methodology was illustrated through a numerical example.

This work paves the ways for future research on quantized sampled-data control design. Extensions to aperiodic sampled-data systems as well as to other classes of quantizers are currently part of our research.

Abstract: In this paper, a two-stage method for finding amplitudes and phases of single-modulus components is presented. It is based on the quantum superposition principle of squeezing wave.

In this paper, we propose a two-stage model for detecting the amplitude and phase of a single-modulus component. The model is based on the quantum superposition principle of squeezing wave. The method takes one input oscillograph measurement times t seconds. The method assumes that the target signal is a single-modulus component with amplitude and phase that are the superposition of two components. The signals of the two components are inverted and measured using a combined set of single-modulus components. First, a set of input signals (both amplitude and phase) is measured using the toy EXODE model. The target amplitude and phase are then estimated using the one-stage fit rule. Next, the toy EXODE model is redefined to meet the two-stage model as Conditions (i) and (ii) match Conditions (i) and (ii). Finally, the one-stage detection method to demodulate the target signal is extended to a two-stage one. The one-stage method yields a 2-degree of freedom amplitude-phase transformation relation between the amplitude and phase of the single-modulus component and a sinusoidal oscillator. A drawing of the method is presented which illustrates how the one-stage hybrid algorithm converges.
